visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through
quiz.answers_at: Answers. One: eight hundred plus three hundred

questions.q: Equity value 800, debt 300, cash 100, non-controlling interests 50. What's the enterprise value?
questions.explain: 800 + 300 − 100 + 50 = 1,050. Minority interests are added, not subtracted.
questions.explain_at: Start with equity value. Then add debt

questions.q: Enterprise value 1,000, debt 400, cash 50, nothing else. What's the equity value?
questions.explain: Going back from EV, everything flips: 1,000 − 400 + 50 = 650. Subtracting the cash gives 550.
questions.explain_at: Going from enterprise value back to equity, everything flips

questions.q: A company owns 30% of another business. On the bridge, what do you do with that stake?
questions.explain: The stake isn't consolidated, so its EBITDA isn't in the numbers, but its value is in the share price: take it out.
questions.explain_at: The mirror image. Cafe Group owns only twenty percent

questions.q: Why do you add non-controlling interests to get enterprise value?

options.text: Because they're a claim that ranks ahead of debt
Because minority holders are paid dividends before the parent
Because consolidated EBITDA includes the whole subsidiary
Because they're a form of cash held by the subsidiary

questions.explain: The parent consolidates 100% of the subsidiary's EBITDA even though it owns less, so EV must include the part owned by outsiders or the multiple won't match.
questions.explain_at: That's the trap, and it's the most common mistake on this whole topic. You add it

questions.q: A company reports EBITDA after rent. Should its enterprise value include lease liabilities?

options.text: Yes, IFRS 16 puts them on the balance sheet
Yes, if the company rents its shops

questions.explain: If rent is already a cost in EBITDA, adding lease liabilities to EV counts the leases twice. Match the two, as Rexel's EBITDAaL does.
questions.explain_at: If you use EBITDA after rent, you leave leases out
